title: Sentiri RAG Evaluation Does the Chatbot Retrieve the Right Evidence?
text:
The pipeline under evaluation
question → embed (MiniLM multilingual)
         → ChromaDB cosine top-20          ── dense recall (cheap, broad)
         → cross-encoder rerank → top-5    ── precision (slow, sharp)
         → grounded LLM answer + citations ── generation (Groq)

Two stages fail in different ways: retrieval misses the evidence,


generation ignores or overreaches it: so each is evaluated separately.

According to our pipeline we use dense embeddings setup and NOT BM25 setup why ? lets dive into it
Firstly, we need to understand where and how to use Best Match 25 ? in our architecture ?
question → tokenize (lowercase, Sastrawi stem)  ── query must see the
                                                   same preprocessing as
                                                   the index, or scores die
         → BM25 score vs inverted index  ── lexical recall (cheap, broad)
              (term freq × idf ÷ doc length)
         → top-20 candidate chunk ids
         → cross-encoder rerank → top-5     ── precision (slow, sharp)
         → grounded LLM answer + citations  ── generation (Groq)


Index side (built once, offline):


chunks → tokenize (same pipeline!) → inverted index:
         term → [(chunk_id, tf, doc_len)]


And since the real-world version is usually hybrid, the full picture:


  == BELOW SHOWS THE DIFFERENCES BETWEEN USING DENSE EMBEDDINGS PIPELINE VS BM-25 ==

                 ┌─ embed → ChromaDB cosine top-20 ─┐
question ────────┤                                  ├→ fuse (RRF) → top-20
                 └─ tokenize → BM25 top-20 ─────────┘        → rerank → top-5
                                                               → LLM + citations


The full strategy of building this RAG pipeline

FILE: chat_analyzer/services/rag_service.py
Ported from PersonalRAG, one key change (multilingual embedding for Malay).

MODELS
  Embedding: paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 (SentenceTransformer, 384-dim, lazy singleton)
  Reranker:  cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 (CrossEncoder, lazy singleton)
  LLM:       Groq openai/gpt-oss-120b, temp 0.1, max_tokens 1024 (GROQ_API_KEY env-only)

STORE
  ChromaDB PersistentClient, dir data/vector_store/
  Collection "treatment_documents", hnsw:space=cosine
  Chunk ids: md5(doc_title)[:8] + index → e.g. "9349f30a_3" (these are your gold-set annotation ids)

CONFIG (hardcoded constants, not env)
  CHUNK_SIZE 1000 chars, CHUNK_OVERLAP 200
  TOP_K 5 (post-rerank), RETRIEVE_K 20 (dense recall), SCORE_THRESHOLD 0.2

INGEST (ingest_document, called by Celery on doctor upload)
  load_and_chunk: PyMuPDFLoader (PDF) / TextLoader (.txt/.md) →
    RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(1000/200, default separators) →
    metadata {source, page, chunk_index}
  embed_and_store: batch encode → collection.add(ids, embeddings, documents,
    metadata {source, page, chunk_index, doc_title, document_id?})
  Returns IngestionResult {status: ready|failed, chunks_created, error}
  document_id links chunks → TreatmentDocument row → file_url for citations

QUERY (query(), called by chatbot view)
  1. retrieve(question, top_k=20): encode query → ChromaDB cosine query →
     cosine distance→similarity = (2-d)/2 → filter similarity < 0.2 → RetrievedChunk
  2. rerank(query, docs, top_k=5): CrossEncoder.predict on (query, content) pairs →
     sort desc by rerank_score → top 5
  3. build_context: numbered [Document i - title, page (relevance: X%)] headers
  4. build_sources: {title, page, score, preview[:200], file_url} —
     single TreatmentDocument query (no N+1)
  5. calculate_confidence: sigmoid(max rerank score)
  6. generate_answer: Malay system prompt (grounded-only, refuse if insufficient,
     match answer language to question) + context + question → Groq
  Returns RAGResponse {answer, sources, confidence, context?}

UTILITIES
  get_collection_stats(): chunk count for dashboard
  delete_document_chunks(doc_title): where={doc_title} filter → delete

KNOWN STATE
  Collection: 14 chunks / 3 PDFs (annotated gold ids from col.get())
  Reranker: caught degrading hit@5 1.00→0.64 in eval, currently still in the
    pipeline path (fix-or-remove verdict pending — BGE-m3 one-line swap is the fix)








Note



BGE-M3 (Chen et al. 2024)? what is it ?

Paper: Chen, Xiao, Zhang, Luo, Lian, Liu (2024). “BGE M3-Embedding: Multi-Lingual, Multi-Functionality, Multi-Granularity Text Embeddings Through Self-Knowledge Distillation.” arXiv:2402.03216
Model card: https://huggingface.co/BAAI/bge-m3
Code: https://github.com/FlagOpen/FlagEmbedding (FlagEmbedding/BGE_M3)


An embedding model from BAAI Beijing Ai Academy m3 means = three multi’s


Multi-Functionality: one model, three retrieval modes — dense, sparse (lexical), multi-vector (ColBERT-style) — trained via unified fine-tuning with self-knowledge distillation from all three. The sparse output is a vocab-sized vector, mostly zeros, weight per token present in the text — same family as BM25/uniCOIL/SPLADE but learned.
Multi-Linguality: 100+ working languages.
Multi-Granularity: inputs from short sentences up to 8192 tokens.
Concrete spec: 1024-dim embeddings (vs MiniLM’s 384), max_length 8192, architecture = xlm-roberta-large extended to 8192 and further pretrained with RetroMAE, then contrastive learning (bge-m3-unsupervised), then unified fine-tuning.

But first we will use standard ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2

title: Sentiri RAG Evaluation Does the Chatbot Retrieve the Right Evidence?
section: The headline finding: the reranker is not earning its latency
text:
The headline finding: the reranker is not earning its latency
Dense retrieval is excellent: hit@20 is perfect — for all 11 real questions, the embedding model places at least one gold chunk inside the top-20 candidates. The funnel mouth never misses.
The cross-encoder rerank then reduces quality: MRR drops from 0.56 to 0.44, hit@5 falls 0.82→0.73 (3 of 11 questions lose gold from the top-5), and the stricter recall@5 — all gold chunks inside the window, not just one — falls 0.77→0.59. The failure mode is displacement: dense retrieval hands the reranker gold in strong positions (rank 1, 3, 4) and the cross-encoder demotes it below rank 5. Worst case — “why does my autistic child only want to eat one brand of food” — gold sat at dense rank 1 and rerank pushed it out of the top 5.
The failures are not language-bound (2 English, 2 Malay), so “English-trained reranker (ms-marco-MiniLM) struggles with Malay” is only part of the diagnosis. The reranker is also credited with two rank-3 → rank-1 rescues — it wins some questions and loses others, net negative on this gold set.

title: Sentiri RAG Evaluation Does the Chatbot Retrieve the Right Evidence?
text:
Improvements, in evidence order

Equal-k comparison first: score dense top-5 vs rerank top-5 on the same footing before any removal decision (the harness supports this with two extra metric calls).
Swap the cross-encoder for a multilingual reranker (BGE-m3 family) and re-run — the eval harness makes this a one-line change plus one 37-second re-run. The numbers decide.
Gate rerank by question language if the swap does not close the gap.

title: Sentiri RAG Evaluation Does the Chatbot Retrieve the Right Evidence?
section: Adversarial questions: retrieval cannot detect them
text:
Adversarial questions: retrieval cannot detect them
Both adversarial questions retrieve chunks with similarity 0.79–0.85 — nearly as high as real questions. With SCORE_THRESHOLD = 0.2, the retrieval layer passes them through confidently; the only barrier to a hallucinated answer (invented therapy costs) is the LLM choosing to refuse. Refusal accuracy is therefore a generation-layer metric, not a retrieval one.


Code
import json
import pandas as pd

with open("rag_eval_results.json") as f:
    res = json.load(f)
agg = res["aggregate"]

# Collect-then-score: the equal-k dense metrics are recomputed from the
# saved evidence (dense_ranked_ids per record) — no pipeline re-run needed.
def hit_at_k(ranked_ids: list[str], gold_ids: list[str], k: int) -> int:
    return 1 if set(gold_ids) & set(ranked_ids[:k]) else 0

def precision_at_k(ranked_ids: list[str], gold_ids: list[str], k: int) -> float:
    return len(set(ranked_ids[:k]) & set(gold_ids)) / k

def recall_at_k(ranked_ids: list[str], gold_ids: list[str], k: int) -> float:
    """Strict companion to hit@k: ALL gold must be inside top-k, not just one."""
    return len(set(ranked_ids[:k]) & set(gold_ids)) / len(gold_ids)

real = [r for r in res["records"] if not r["adversarial"]]
dense_hit5 = sum(hit_at_k(r["dense_ranked_ids"], r["gold_chunk_ids"], 5) for r in real) / len(real)
dense_p5 = sum(precision_at_k(r["dense_ranked_ids"], r["gold_chunk_ids"], 5) for r in real) / len(real)
dense_rec5 = sum(recall_at_k(r["dense_ranked_ids"], r["gold_chunk_ids"], 5) for r in real) / len(real)
rerank_rec5 = sum(recall_at_k(r["rerank_ranked_ids"], r["gold_chunk_ids"], 5) for r in real) / len(real)
gold_lost_rerank = sum(
    1 for r in real
    if recall_at_k(r["dense_ranked_ids"], r["gold_chunk_ids"], 5) == 1.0
    and recall_at_k(r["rerank_ranked_ids"], r["gold_chunk_ids"], 5) < 1.0
)

# Every number followed by its interpretation — the table argues,
# not just reports.
df = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Metric": "Hit@20", "Dense only": agg["hit@20"], "Dense + rerank": None,
     "Reading": "perfect — gold reaches the top-20 for all 11 real questions"},
    {"Metric": "Hit@5", "Dense only": agg["hit@5"], "Dense + rerank": agg["hit@5_rerank"],
     "Reading": "3/11 questions lose gold from the top-5 after reranking"},
    {"Metric": "Recall@5", "Dense only": dense_rec5, "Dense + rerank": rerank_rec5,
     "Reading": f"strict: ALL gold inside top-5 — rerank evicts the sole gold chunk on {gold_lost_rerank} questions (recall 1.0→0.0)"},
    {"Metric": "MRR", "Dense only": agg["mrr_dense"], "Dense + rerank": agg["mrr_rerank"],
     "Reading": "rerank demotes gold on average — MRR drops"},
    {"Metric": "Precision@5", "Dense only": agg["precision@5"], "Dense + rerank": agg["precision@5_rerank"],
     "Reading": "precision@k is capped at 1/k"},
])

title: Sentiri Model Evaluation: Why XLM-RoBERTa and BERTopic?
text:
1.1 The resource gap (weaker argument)
Malay has no maintained, ready-to-use sentiment lexicon — nothing comparable to English’s VADER, SentiWordNet, or AFINN that one can download and run today. What exists are induction methods in research papers (Omar et al. 2017 maps WordNet Bahasa onto English SentiWordNet; cross-lingual synset-mapping experiments exist), whose outputs are not published as reusable artifacts. This is a real but recoverable obstacle — one could build a domain lexicon — so it alone does not justify abandoning the approach. The decisive arguments follow.

title: Sentiri Model Evaluation: Why XLM-RoBERTa and BERTopic?
section: 1.2 Contextual polarity flips — the measured failure mode
text:
1.2 Contextual polarity flips — the measured failure mode
A lexicon assigns each word a prior polarity (dictionary meaning). But words carry their contextual polarity from the sentence. In therapy-progress chats, this gap is not an edge case — we measured it:


Code
# df_raw / train_df / test_df come from the data-split cell (shared split).

POS_WORDS = ["bagus", "baik", "gembira", "syukur", "senang", "best",
             "pandai", "bijak", "boleh", "suka", "terer", "hebat"]
pattern = "|".join(POS_WORDS)

traps = df_raw[(df_raw["label"] == 0)
               & (df_raw["text"].str.lower().str.contains(pattern, na=False))]
n_neg = (df_raw["label"] == 0).sum()
print(f"Negative messages containing a positive-looking word: "
      f"{len(traps)} / {n_neg} ({100*len(traps)/n_neg:.1f}%)")
traps["text"].head(12).tolist()


Negative messages containing a positive-looking word: 99 / 743 (13.3%)

 'dia selalu sedih dan suka marah, merajuk.']


The recurring patterns in these messages — the reasons word-level lookup fails:








Trap
Example from our data
Why a lexicon cannot see it




Negation
“merangkak pun tak boleh”
boleh scores positive; the tak before it flips the phrase. Lexicons score words one at a time


Contrastive conjunction
“ammar boleh membaca tetapi tidak boleh berinteraksi”
First clause positive, whole sentence negative — polarity lives in the contrast, not any single word


Mixed-clause polarity
“dia selalu sedih dan suka marah, merajuk”
suka (“likes”) attaches to a negative behavior: “easily angered”


Domain semantics
“dia masih tak boleh control”
Progress-report framing makes capability words markers of struggle when negated



This is the prior vs contextual polarity distinction (Wilson, Wiebe & Hoffmann, 2005): lexicons capture the former, sentiment in real text is carried by the latter. A transformer reads the whole sequence and learns these flips from labeled data — including that “tidur lewat” is a complaint, not a nap report.

1.3 Lexicon baseline — measured, not assumed
To honor the suggestion properly, we test it rather than dismiss it. The baseline below scores messages using our curated sentiment word lists (the same domain knowledge embedded in domain_words_sentiment.txt) — the strongest lexicon a lexicon approach could reasonably have here.

title: Sentiri Model Evaluation: Why XLM-RoBERTa and BERTopic?
text:
1.4 Lexicon baseline results


Code
# Lexicon baseline: the strongest lexicon approach this domain could have.
# Word lists are curated from our domain knowledge (same knowledge that lives
# in domain_words_sentiment.txt). Zero-hit rule: predict NEUTRAL — the lexicon
# sees no sentiment signal, and "no signal" is the definition of neutral.
# This is deliberately FAVORABLE to the baseline (not a strawman).

POS_WORDS = ["bagus", "baik", "gembira", "syukur", "senang", "best",
             "pandai", "bijak", "boleh", "suka", "terer", "hebat",
             "alhamdulillah", "ceria", "bangga", "tahniah",
             "maju", "improve", "progress", "cemerlang", "mantap"]
NEG_WORDS = ["sedih", "marah", "menangis", "nangis", "takut", "raung",
             "merajuk", "stress", "penat", "susah", "payah", "berat",
             "kena", "aduh", "gelisah", "resah", "bimbang", "risau",
             "buruk", "teruk", "malas", "degil", "nakal", "kasar"]

def lexicon_predict(text: str) -> int:
    t = str(text).lower()
    pos = sum(1 for w in POS_WORDS if w in t)
    neg = sum(1 for w in NEG_WORDS if w in t)
    if pos > neg:
        return 2      # positive
    if neg > pos:
        return 0      # negative
    return 1          # neutral — zero hits or tie: no signal = neutral (fair rule)

# NOTE: no split here — the shared split (seed=42, stratified) was created once

lex_acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
lex_f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred, average="macro")

# The key number: performance on the trap subset (negative messages

Reading the table: even with the favorable zero-hit rule (no sentiment words → neutral, which scores free hits on logistical smalltalk), the lexicon barely reaches coin-flip accuracy (49.4%). On the trap messages — negative messages containing positive-looking words — it predicts positive on 17 of 20 and negative on none: 0.000 accuracy. Wilson 95% CI on 0/20: [0, 16.8%] — so the defensible claim is “under 17% on traps at 95% confidence,” not “0% forever.” This is the failure mode of prior-polarity lookup measured on our own data: the words are positive, the sentences are not, and no word-level scorer can see the difference. A fine-tuned transformer reads the whole sequence — that is the hypothesis Part 2 tests.

2.2 Fine-tune XLM-R (the incumbent)

title: Sentiri Model Evaluation: Why XLM-RoBERTa and BERTopic?
text:
The decision — honestly stated
mBERT wins on raw accuracy (0.882 vs 0.863, +1.9pp) and macro-F1 (0.881 vs 0.862). It is also 1.6× smaller (178M vs 278M params). On paper, mBERT is the stronger model.
But the choice was not “best accuracy” — it was “best fit for clinical requirements.” R3 (negative recall) is the priority metric in a therapy context: missing a distressed message is a clinical risk. XLM-R wins negative recall (0.933 vs 0.919), and on the 20 trap messages — the hardest cases where a lexicon scored 0.000 — XLM-R scored 0.950. That is the gap that matters for this domain.
The 1.9pp overall accuracy difference translates to roughly 8 additional messages correctly classified by mBERT out of 432. The negative-recall gap (1.3pp) is about 2 messages. These are small sample differences — we report them honestly rather than over-claiming. The defensible position is: XLM-R was chosen for its strength on the clinical priority (R3) and the hardest cases (traps), accepting a small overall-accuracy trade-off. If deployment cost were the overriding concern, mBERT would be the equally defensible choice.

text:
3.1 Why topic modeling at all (vs. keyword rules alone)
The initial approach — keyword matching against 12 seed keyword lists — works for unambiguous messages. But our production data shows that 112 of 266 conversations (42%) are assigned to multiple topics simultaneously. These are messages whose words span multiple domains: “tantrum tidur pujuk” touches Behaviour, Sleep, and Therapy Progress at once.
A pure keyword rule says “this message matches 3 topics” and stops — it cannot decide which is primary. The hybrid pipeline (coverage override → cluster inheritance → outlier fallback) resolves these ambiguities, but only because BERTopic provides the cluster structure that keyword rules lack. Without clustering, every multi-match is a tie; with clustering, the message inherits the topic of the cluster its embedding neighbors belong to.

title: Sentiri Model Evaluation: Why XLM-RoBERTa and BERTopic?
text:
3.2 Why BERTopic specifically
Three architectural properties make BERTopic the right choice for this domain:








Property
What it does
Why it matters here




Transformer embeddings
xlm-roberta-large converts each message into a 1024-dim semantic vector
Messages with the same meaning but different words cluster together — “menangis sampai buka balutan” and “nangis lama sangat” are semantically close despite sharing no content words


UMAP + HDBSCAN
UMAP reduces dimensions (1024→5); HDBSCAN finds dense clusters and labels sparse points as outliers (-1)
K-means forces every point into a cluster — a message about “makan” (eating) gets shoved into the nearest cluster even if it doesn’t fit. HDBSCAN allows outliers, so ambiguous messages stay unmapped until the fallback rules handle them


c-TF-IDF
Class-based TF-IDF generates interpretable topic labels from cluster word frequencies
The admin sees “tidur, malam, tidur lewat” as a topic name and can promote it to “Sleep and Routine” — the names are human-readable, not opaque cluster IDs




The ‘tidur’ case study (Run 8 evidence)
In Run 7, the word “tidur” (sleep) was inherited by the Therapy Progress cluster because HDBSCAN had blobbed short texts into a single large cluster. Run 8’s seed de-overlap + coverage override fix (Door 1) detected that “tidur” appears in exactly one topic’s seed list (Sleep and Routine) and overrode the cluster inheritance, assigning it correctly. This is the hybrid pipeline working as designed: BERTopic clusters provide the structure, supervised seed keywords provide the correction.

3.3 Topic coherence (c_v)
Coherence measures whether the top words in each topic actually co-occur in the corpus — i.e., whether the topic makes semantic sense. We compute c_v using gensim CoherenceModel (preferred) over the 136-document corpus. This replaces the earlier NPMI approximation.
Two sets of topics are evaluated:

Discovered topics — top words extracted by BERTopic clustering (unsupervised)
Defined topics — seed keyword lists curated from domain expert knowledge (supervised)

The comparison reveals whether unsupervised discovery or expert-informed structure produces more semantically coherent topics at this corpus size.

title: Sentiri Model Evaluation: Why XLM-RoBERTa and BERTopic?
text:
3.5 BERTopic vs alternatives







Approach
Why not for this domain




LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation)
Assumes documents are “bags of words” — word order doesn’t matter. Short WhatsApp messages (3-10 tokens) give LDA almost nothing to work with. Also requires pre-specifying K (number of topics); BERTopic discovers K from the data


K-means clustering
Forces every message into a cluster. Ambiguous messages get misassigned with no “I don’t know” option. HDBSCAN’s -1 outlier label is critical for the hybrid pipeline’s fallback mechanism


Pure keyword rules
The 42% multi-topic rate proves rules alone can’t resolve ambiguity. Rules are the first door (coverage override), not the whole house


Top2Vec
Also embedding-based, but doesn’t use c-TF-IDF for interpretable names. The admin-facing topic names (which can be promoted/reviewed) are a product requirement BERTopic uniquely satisfies



The hybrid pipeline is the real defense: BERTopic is not used alone. Coverage override (Door 1) handles unambiguous messages with zero ML compute. Cluster inheritance (Door 2) handles the 88% of messages that fall into a clear cluster. Outlier fallback (Door 3) handles the sparse points HDBSCAN flagged as -1. Each door has an exit condition; the pipeline combines supervised (keyword seeds) and unsupervised (BERTopic clustering) approaches — which is why it outperforms either alone.

Lets dive into this one by one col. ?

1.”Chunks pass threshold”=20
We asked for top-20 chunks, so all 20 chunks scored similarity >= 0.5, because our cutoff is 0.2, so all 20 survive.
========================
2. “Top chunk” = 7a2ee7cf_3
This is just the ID of the chunk that ranked #1 for this question. It’s name not a score yet. Which chunk is it?
7a2ee7cf_3 is the speech therapy doc, chunk 3 - the one containing “2-3 kali seminggu, 45min-1jam” (session frequency/duration)
So when a parent asks about PRICE, the #1 chunk retrieval grabs is the one about how OFTEN sessions happen.
Related topic, wrong content.>
3.”Top similarity” = 0.710
This is ChromaDB’s cosine similarity between the question’s embedding and that top chunk’s embedding,
converted from distance. It answers: “how confident does DENSE retrieval feel about this top chunk?” 0.710 on a 0-1 scale (roughly).
For context, REAL questions that got correctly answered
their top similarities are in the same ballpark (Q10 even scored 0.846!).
That’s the punchline of this column: the similarity score for an unanswerable question (0.71, 0.85)
is indistinguishable from the score for an answerable one.
The number LOOKS confident but means nothing: similarity measures topic closeness (“therapy”),
not answer presence (“price”). A similarity threshold can never separate these.
** 4.”Top rerank score” = 2.305 (Q9) vs -4.103 (Q10)**
This is the cross-encoder’s score for the (question, top chunk) pair.
It answers a DIFFERENT question than similarity: “does this chunk actually ANSWER this question?”
the cross-encoder reads both texts together, so it grades relevance, not topic. Scale: unbounded, roughly anything positive = “this looks like an answer”, strongly negative = “this does not answer it.”
Q10: -4.1 → the reranker says loud and clear “this chunk does NOT answer ‘what age to start intervention’.” Correct judgment.
Q9: +2.3 → the reranker says “yes, this looks relevant to ‘how much do sessions cost’” — WRONG judgment, because frequency and cost are lexically close (“berapa kerap” vs “berapa kos”). The reranker got fooled on the near-miss.

CautionWhat to add to our gold set of question ? [click here]





Current set: 13 questions (11 real + 2 adversarial). Dense retrieval is at ceiling on it — hit@20 = 1.00, so no embedding change can show improvement on questions that are already all retrieved. New questions must be designed to break the ceiling, each targeting a named failure mode:

Multi-hop (2 gold chunks, different docs) — the visible gap. Questions whose answer needs evidence from two documents, e.g. a feeding problem that is treated WITH a communication approach (“anak saya tolak makan sebab tak reti nak minta — apa nak buat?” → feeding chunk + AAC/PECS chunk). Current set has no question with gold chunks in two different docs. Tests: can retrieval surface BOTH, or does one topic dominate?
Hard paraphrase (zero lexical overlap). Q2 tested mild paraphrase (“tunggu giliran” vs “gilir bercakap”). Next level: questions that share no words with the gold chunk — pure semantics (“anak saya buat hal bila tak dapat apa dia nak” for the screaming/tantrum chunk, where the doc says “menjerit” / “challenging behaviour”). Tests: how far can paraphrase go before dense retrieval breaks?
Cross-lingual, hard mode. Q3/Q12 are English→Malay-doc, but on easy topics. Add one where the English question uses vocabulary that never appears in the Malay chunk. Tests: the embedding space’s cross-lingual depth, which is exactly what a BGE-m3 swap claims to improve.
Near-miss adversarial (the Q9 trap, weaponized). Current adversarial questions fail cleanly. Add ones where retrieval DOES find topic-adjacent content that plausibly-but-wrongly answers (e.g. a medication-dosage or therapy-qualification question near the session-frequency chunk). Tests: refusal under real temptation — the generation-layer failure case, not the easy one.
Expanded refusal set (adversarial, easy mode, quantity). 5–8 more unanswerable questions (prices, locations, doctor names, legal, vaccine) so refusal accuracy becomes a real n, not n=2.

Plan: ~8–10 new questions total, old 13 kept (regression check — pipeline runs in ~37s). Annotate gold chunk ids by hand from col.get() as before, freeze the set, rerun. THEN the BGE-m3 embedding swap has measurable room to help — and if it doesn’t, that’s a finding too.
Order matters: gold set first (the instrument), model swap second (the treatment). Otherwise the swap verdict is meaningless.
